title: Volunteering and health
hook: volunteers had lower mortality in a review, though healthier people may volunteer more

segments.voice: Yesterday: purpose and long life, and Marcus Aurelius rising to the work of a human being. Your line was purpose. Did you write your one line down? Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

A clipboard hangs by the door of a food bank. Names, phone numbers, a column for shifts. Saturday, nine to eleven. Somebody's handwriting is neat, somebody's is a scrawl. Sheets like this hang in church halls, animal shelters, libraries and gurdwaras. Researchers have asked a blunt question about the people whose names end up on them: do they live longer? They found an answer, and then had to qualify it carefully.
screen: `A CLIPBOARD BY THE DOOR.` → `SATURDAY, NINE TO ELEVEN.` → `DO THEY LIVE LONGER?`

segments.voice: First, the finding. Morris Okun and colleagues gathered studies on older adults and volunteering and pooled them in a review in the journal Psychology and Aging. Across those studies, older people who volunteered had lower death rates over the years they were followed. Second, the catch, and it's a big one. You have to be fairly well to stand at a food bank for two hours. So healthier people may simply volunteer more, and that alone could make volunteers look longer-lived. When the researchers accounted for health and other factors, the gap got smaller, though it didn't vanish. The honest summary: a real link, with the direction still argued over. Third, a word for it from one tradition. Sikhs call selfless service seva. In gurdwaras, volunteers cook and serve in the langar, the free kitchen where anyone can sit and eat. In Sikh teaching, seva is done without looking for a reward, and that includes a health reward. The dal is stirred for the guests, not for anyone's lifespan. Fourth, a line from Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet, from the section on giving: "You give but little when you give of your possessions. It is when you give of yourself that you truly give." An hour is exactly that kind of gift. You can't wire it. You have to show up. The science says volunteers tend to do well. The traditions say the point is the person on the other side of the table. Both fit in one Saturday shift. Give an hour.
screen: `VOLUNTEERS, LOWER DEATH RATES.` · `HEALTHIER PEOPLE MAY VOLUNTEER MORE.` · `SEVA: SERVICE WITHOUT REWARD.` · then, large: `WHEN YOU GIVE OF YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your hour. Sit comfortably and breathe. Then let one face come to mind: someone who could use an hour of somebody's time. A neighbor who can't carry groceries. A kitchen that feeds people. A kid who needs a reader. A shelter, a clean-up, a phone call to someone alone. Don't pick the most impressive option. Pick the one you would actually do. Then choose roughly when. Hold that person or place in mind for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Volunteering and health. A real link, with a catch: healthier people may volunteer more. And a week ends: cold water, yoga, tai chi, sleep, nature, purpose, service. Seven honest looks. Today's word.
Your line: give an hour. Today, make the call, send the message or sign the sheet that puts your hour on a real day. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, the word Sikhs use for work like cooking and serving in the langar.

trapdoor: what you thought: volunteering is good for your health. done.
what it means: in a review of studies, older volunteers had lower death rates, but healthier people may volunteer more in the first place.
what a scholar hears: a meta-analysis of observational studies. adjusting for health and other factors shrank the effect without erasing it, and the direction of cause is still debated.
